blocks.text: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as an abnormality of kidney structure or function, present for **at least 3 months**, with implications for health.
CKD is characterised by persistent reduction in kidney function, evidence of kidney damage, or both.
It may progress to kidney failure, requiring renal replacement therapy (dialysis or kidney transplantation).
CKD is diagnosed when one or both of the following abnormalities persist for at least 3 months:
**A. Reduced glomerular filtration rate**
**B. Markers of kidney damage**

blocks.title: One or more of the following:

items.text: Albuminuria: urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) ≥30 mg/g (≥3 mg/mmol).
Electrolyte abnormalities due to tubular disorders.

blocks.text: **Important:** An eGFR of 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m² alone does not establish CKD unless another marker of kidney damage is present.
Similarly, a single abnormal creatinine or urine ACR does not establish chronic disease without evidence of persistence or other reliable evidence of chronicity.
This is known as the **CGA classification**.
**Clinical significance:** Increasing albuminuria is associated with increased cardiovascular risk and progression of kidney disease, even when eGFR is relatively preserved.

**Diagnosis: CKD G3a A3.**

blocks.title: The major objectives of CKD treatment are:

items.text: Slow the progression of kidney disease.
Reduce albuminuria and intraglomerular pressure where appropriate.
Optimise glycaemic control in diabetic patients.
Prevent and treat CKD-mineral and bone disorder.
Preserve nutritional status and quality of life.
Prepare patients appropriately for dialysis or transplantation when necessary.

blocks.text: Unlike AKI, CKD is generally managed through long-term kidney protection and complication prevention.
However, patients with advanced CKD may develop emergencies requiring immediate treatment.

blocks.text: **Important precautions**

items.text: Check serum creatinine and potassium before starting.
Recheck BP, creatinine and potassium within 2–4 weeks after initiation or dose escalation.
A creatinine increase of up to 30% within 4 weeks may be acceptable if there is no other concerning clinical finding.
Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
Reduce or discontinue if there is symptomatic hypotension or uncontrolled hyperkalaemia despite appropriate treatment.

SGLT2 inhibitors reduce proximal tubular glucose and sodium reabsorption, restoring tubuloglomerular feedback and reducing intraglomerular pressure.
They reduce the risk of CKD progression and cardiovascular events.

Blood pressure control is essential in slowing CKD progression.
**Target:**
KDIGO suggests a systolic BP target below 120 mmHg in adults with CKD and hypertension, when tolerated, using standardised office BP measurement.
This target should not be applied uncritically to routine non-standardised measurements or patients with symptomatic hypotension, frailty or other contraindications.

**B. Insulin**
Insulin requirements may decrease as CKD advances because renal insulin clearance is reduced.

items.text: Insulin glargine: Individualised SC dose once daily.
Insulin aspart: Individualised SC dose before meals.
Regular insulin: Individualised according to glucose profile.

blocks.text: There is no universal CKD-specific starting dose. Titrate according to blood glucose and hypoglycaemia risk.
**C. GLP-1 receptor agonists**

In adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD who do not achieve individualised glycaemic targets despite metformin and SGLT2 therapy, or cannot use these medications, a long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist with cardiovascular benefit is recommended.
CKD significantly increases cardiovascular risk.
Statin therapy is recommended for many adults with non-dialysis CKD, particularly those aged 50 years and above.
**Prescription: Atorvastatin**
Increase to 40–80 mg when indicated by cardiovascular risk and tolerability.
In adults aged 18–49 years, consider statin therapy according to diabetes, established cardiovascular disease, previous ischaemic stroke and estimated cardiovascular risk.
For patients already receiving maintenance dialysis, initiation of a statin is not routinely recommended solely because of dialysis status; continuation of existing therapy may be appropriate.
CKD may cause metabolic acidosis because of impaired renal acid excretion.
Consider pharmacological treatment, with or without dietary intervention, when serum bicarbonate is sufficiently low to have clinical implications.
KDIGO 2024 gives bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L in adults as an example of a level warranting consideration.
**Prescription: Sodium bicarbonate tablets**

items.text: Starting dose: 500 mg orally two or three times daily.

blocks.text: Titrate according to serum bicarbonate, BP, sodium concentration and volume status.

Anaemia in CKD is commonly caused by reduced renal erythropoietin production, iron deficiency, inflammation and shortened red cell survival.

Consider when oral iron is not tolerated, ineffective or inadequate, or when IV iron is preferred in haemodialysis patients.

In adults, ESA initiation is individualised, generally when haemoglobin is approximately 90–100 g/L, depending on symptoms, transfusion risk and cardiovascular/thrombotic risk.
Avoid targeting a normal haemoglobin concentration with ESA therapy because this increases cardiovascular and thrombotic risks.

Reduce excessive intake of highly absorbable phosphate additives and processed foods.

**Prescription: Sevelamer carbonate**

items.text: Dose: Commonly 500–1,000 mg orally with meals, adjusted according to elemental calcium content and phosphate level.

blocks.text: Avoid excessive calcium loading, particularly in patients with hypercalcaemia or vascular calcification.
**C. Vitamin D**
Cholecalciferol may be prescribed when nutritional vitamin D deficiency is present.
Active vitamin D analogues such as calcitriol are reserved for selected patients, particularly those with severe progressive secondary hyperparathyroidism in advanced CKD.
Do not prescribe calcitriol routinely to all patients with CKD.

items.text: Reduce excessive dietary sodium; a target below 2 g sodium daily (approximately 5 g salt) is reasonable for many adults.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Advanced CKD and renal replacement therapy

blocks.text: Patients with progressive CKD should receive education and preparation before kidney failure develops.

blocks.text: Dialysis initiation is not determined by eGFR alone.
**1. Haemodialysis**
Blood is circulated through an extracorporeal filter to remove excess fluid and waste products.
Usually performed several times weekly in maintenance programmes.
**2. Peritoneal dialysis**
Uses the peritoneum as a semipermeable membrane. It can be performed at home following appropriate training.
**3. Kidney transplantation**
Provides renal replacement through a transplanted kidney and is an important treatment option for eligible patients with kidney failure.

blocks.text: **20 essential CKD facts**

items.text: CKD requires abnormalities of kidney structure or function lasting at least 3 months.
eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for at least 3 months establishes CKD.
G1 and G2 require additional evidence of kidney damage.
CKD classification uses CGA: Cause, GFR and Albuminuria.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs are important in albuminuric CKD.
Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB routinely.
Check potassium and creatinine after starting RAS blockade.
SGLT2 inhibitors provide kidney protection beyond glucose lowering.
Finerenone is useful in selected patients with diabetic CKD and persistent albuminuria.
CKD-associated anaemia is commonly normocytic and normochromic.
Iron deficiency should be addressed before or alongside ESA treatment.
Dialysis is based on clinical indications, not a creatinine threshold alone.
Reassess kidney function at 3 months after AKI to identify persistent CKD.

rows: Often reduced, but may be normal or enlarged
Often irreversible, although some causes are treatable

blocks.text: **Important exception:** Normal or enlarged kidneys do not exclude CKD. Diabetes, polycystic kidney disease, amyloidosis and infiltrative conditions may produce enlarged kidneys.
